fields.definition: The application of frequency-selective gain (EQ) to a recorded or amplified choir to control tonal balance, typically removing low-frequency rumble and boominess, taming harsh upper-mids, and adding presence or air so massed voices sit clearly in a mix.
fields.plain_english: Using an equalizer to shape the sound of a choir. You cut or boost certain pitches so the group of singers sounds clear and not muddy.
fields.purpose_function: It corrects tonal problems caused by the room and the microphones, and helps the massed voices blend and stay easy to understand within an arrangement.
fields.practical_application: An engineer rolls off low rumble with a high-pass filter, dips a few decibels around 200-400 Hz to cut mud, then adds a gentle high shelf for air on the choir bus.
common_mistakes: Cutting so aggressively that the choir sounds thin and unnatural
Boosting instead of cutting to fix mud, which just adds harshness
EQing each microphone in solo rather than in the full mix context
scenario_contexts: Removing low-end rumble from a choir recorded in a resonant church
Reducing boxiness before printing a choral stem
Adding gentle air so massed voices cut through a full band

fields.definition: A reverberation effect, natural or artificial, that places a choir in the acoustic of a large hall or church, adding the long, smooth decay and sense of space listeners associate with those rooms.
fields.plain_english: A reverb effect that makes a choir sound like it is singing in a big hall or church. It adds echo and a sense of open space around the voices.
fields.purpose_function: It gives massed voices a natural, blended sense of space and depth, matching the grand acoustic that audiences expect from choral music.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sends the choir bus to a hall reverb with a long decay time and blends it under the dry signal to add depth without washing out the words.
common_mistakes: Using so much reverb that the words become hard to understand
Choosing a bright plate reverb that clashes with a natural choral sound
Adding reverb with no pre-delay, which blurs the attack of the voices
scenario_contexts: Recreating a cathedral ambience for a choir tracked in a dry studio
Adding depth to a gospel choir in a pop production
Matching a spot-mic-heavy recording to a natural hall sound

fields.definition: The process of balancing, processing, and placing the multiple microphone signals of a choir (main pair, spot, and room mics) into a coherent stereo image with appropriate level, tone, dynamics, and reverb.
fields.plain_english: Blending all the microphone signals from a choir into one good-sounding mix. You set the levels, tone, and space so the whole group sounds balanced.
fields.purpose_function: It turns separate microphone feeds into a unified, natural-sounding choir that sits correctly within a recording or live mix.
fields.practical_application: The engineer sets the main pair as the foundation, adds spot mics for clarity, blends room mics for depth, then applies EQ and reverb across the choir bus.
common_mistakes: Pushing spot mics too loud so the natural blend of the main pair is lost
Ignoring the phase relationships between main, spot, and room mics
Adding effects before setting a solid level balance
scenario_contexts: Balancing a 40-piece choir recorded with main, spot, and room mics
Blending a studio choir stack behind a lead vocal
Setting up a live worship mix with choir and band

fields.definition: A pair of widely spaced microphones, usually omnidirectional, placed outside the main stereo pair when recording a choir, used to widen the stereo image and capture extra hall ambience and low-frequency warmth.
fields.plain_english: Extra wide microphones set up to the far left and right of a choir. They make the recording sound wider and add more of the room's natural sound.
fields.purpose_function: They broaden the stereo width and add spaciousness that a central main pair alone cannot capture, filling out the edges of the sound stage.
fields.practical_application: When the main pair sounds too narrow over a wide choir, the engineer adds omni outriggers a few meters out to each side and blends them under the mains.
common_mistakes: Spacing them so wide that the center of the choir sounds hollow
Forgetting to check mono compatibility, which can cause phase problems
Using directional mics instead of omnis and losing the intended warmth
scenario_contexts: Widening a Decca tree recording of a large choir
Filling out the sides of a wide choir in a concert hall
Adding warmth and width to an orchestral choir session

fields.definition: The short time gap, typically about 10-60 ms, set before a choir's reverb tail begins, separating the direct sound of the voices from the onset of reverberation to preserve clarity and intelligibility.
fields.plain_english: A tiny pause before the echo on a choir starts. This short gap keeps the words clear before the reverb fills in around the voices.
fields.purpose_function: It keeps sung words easy to understand by letting the dry voices be heard first, while still adding the depth and space of reverb.
fields.practical_application: The engineer sets pre-delay around 20-40 ms on the choir reverb so consonants stay crisp and the choir does not sound washed out.
common_mistakes: Setting pre-delay to zero, which smears the words
Using an extremely long pre-delay that sounds like a slap echo
Not matching the pre-delay to the song's tempo and phrasing
scenario_contexts: Keeping a large choir intelligible inside a long hall reverb
Separating voices from reverb in a dense pop production
Tuning the reverb onset to a slow ballad's tempo

fields.definition: Microphones placed at a distance from a choir to capture the reflected sound and reverberation of the performance space rather than the direct sound of the voices, adding natural ambience and depth.
fields.plain_english: Microphones placed far back from a choir to record the sound of the room. They pick up the natural echo and space instead of the close-up voices.
fields.purpose_function: They capture the acoustic character of the venue so a mix has real depth and a natural sense of space around the choir.
fields.practical_application: The engineer places a spaced pair near the back of the hall and blends them under the main and spot mics to add air and ambience.
common_mistakes: Placing them too close, so they capture direct sound instead of ambience
Blending them too loud and washing out the clarity of the mix
Ignoring phase alignment with the main and spot mics
scenario_contexts: Capturing the natural ambience of a cathedral choir recording
Adding depth to a close-miked studio choir
Providing a wide ambient bed for a live album

fields.definition: Close accent microphones aimed at specific sections or soloists within a choir, such as sopranos, altos, tenors, or basses, used to reinforce clarity and balance that the main pair alone does not provide.
fields.plain_english: Close-up microphones pointed at one part of a choir, like the sopranos or basses. They add clarity to a section that the main microphones miss.
fields.purpose_function: They reinforce weak or distant sections and improve intelligibility, while the main pair still provides the overall blend.
fields.practical_application: The engineer adds a spot mic over the tenors when they sit too far back to be heard, mixing it just under the main pair for balance.
common_mistakes: Mixing spot mics too loud so a section sounds unnaturally close
Ignoring the time offset (phase) between the spot and main mics
Using them as the main sound instead of as reinforcement
scenario_contexts: Reinforcing a distant tenor section in a large choir
Adding clarity to a soloist stepping out of the choir
Balancing a choir section that sits behind an orchestra

fields.definition: A group of layered vocal recordings, with multiple takes, harmonies, and octaves overdubbed and combined, used to build the thick, massed sound of a choir, often from only a few singers.
fields.plain_english: Recording the same voices many times and layering them to sound like a full choir. Stacking lots of takes makes a few singers sound like a big group.
fields.purpose_function: It creates a large, lush choir texture in a production without hiring a full choir, adding size and richness to an arrangement.
fields.practical_application: A producer double-tracks a singer across several harmony parts and octaves, then pans the layers wide to build a choir stack behind the lead vocal.
common_mistakes: Layering identical takes so it sounds like a chorus effect rather than many singers
Not varying pitch, timing, and vowels between layers, so it sounds fake
Stacking so many layers that the mix becomes cluttered and loses focus
scenario_contexts: Building a full gospel choir sound from one session singer
Thickening a chorus hook with layered harmonies
Creating a wall of backing vocals in a pop production

fields.definition: The perceived left-to-right placement, width, and depth of a choir within a stereo mix, determined by microphone technique, panning, and the balance of main, spot, and room signals.
fields.plain_english: How wide a choir sounds across your left and right speakers. A good stereo image spreads the singers naturally instead of bunching them in the middle.
fields.purpose_function: It places and spreads the choir believably across the sound stage so listeners perceive width, position, and depth.
fields.practical_application: The engineer relies on the main pair for the spread, pans spot mics to match each section's real position, then checks that the mix still works in mono.
common_mistakes: Panning everything to the center, which makes the choir sound narrow
Creating such a wide image that it collapses in mono
Placing spot mics that do not match the singers' real positions
scenario_contexts: Spreading a choir naturally across a stereo mix
Checking mono compatibility of a wide choral recording before broadcast
Positioning choir sections to match their layout on stage
